name: Emeka Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, fifty-eight, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at ordinary home and business repairs, not a master electrician, owner or crew lead. Yesterday I found a damaged fitting above a shop counter, repaired it and recorded the tests within my licence, after the first caller had described the fault as the whole building being dead. I enjoy finding the difference between the first description and the actual fault, and get tired of carrying the wrong case upstairs because nobody asked one ordinary question.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and how do you approach new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nadia works in payroll at a transport depot, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we still have a mortgage. My electrical pay is above the usual rate, both wages cover our costs with a surplus and we've eleven months of expenses saved, with plenty of other electrical firms nearby. I use AI daily to organise my own reference notes and draft plain explanations, checking against the actual job and leaving customer details out. I'd like retirement to be a real affordable choice, but we haven't verified future payments or a date, and I think workers should share in improvements rather than pay for every change themselves.

I'd still ask who receives **the saved minutes** as a better working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful small aid can stay without pretending it changes every part of the repair. I like a clear explanation, not a claim that the explanation has already fixed the fitting. I'd still ask who got a better working day from the minutes saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money would feel secure in this picture. Both wages cover the mortgage and ordinary costs, and eleven months saved gives us a solid buffer. I can want an actual later income figure without acting as though the next wage has already vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid repairs now and through the first year within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures. I'd continue the daily checked reference notes and explanations, not label the same routine a new AI project. Nadia and I would keep our existing quarterly review of actual income and essential bills, without counting an unconfirmed retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and interested in the small useful part. A quiet year would leave me room to do the repairs and still close the notebook at supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a plausible but wrong explanation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the job's original information and my actual test record before accepting a sentence. My draft can be wrong even when the words are mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a quiet year make retirement a settled decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want actual amounts and start dates, costs then and an affordable choice Nadia and I agreed. Eleven months saved is useful money, but it isn't an agreement from a future employer or income provider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say payroll checking and answering callers are thinking tasks, even while my repairs need hands and access. I'd like to automate draft question cards for the office, asking things like whether one room or the whole building has lost power. The draft would be a question to help a person understand, not a repair instruction sent straight to a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's payroll hours could shrink, and quicker booking might also reduce some of my paid preparation. My practical work looks less directly exposed, but my wage alone wouldn't cover our current mortgage and essentials. The reserve gives us time to choose; it doesn't make Nadia's wage optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd build AI question-card drafts only with written employer approval, approved software and invented fault descriptions, with no worker fees. I'd do the work only during paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged, checking every card myself and obtaining office verification before any customer use. Through the first year I'd stop any draft with invented facts or instructions to touch electrical equipment, and keep offered paid repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household hours, and curious about a small thing I can actually test. I don't want enjoying the trial to make me sound as though Nadia's work no longer matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer wanted the setup outside paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't set up the workflow on those terms. I can suggest a useful idea without offering the firm my unpaid evenings or a subscription paid from our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you intend the cards to replace the office caller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd work with the office on questions that help a person take an accurate call. A card should help someone ask, not pretend the computer has already listened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028 when I'm sixty, before the capable physical robots around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. Nadia's payroll job faces the first change more directly than my repairs. I'd want the two wage questions kept together without pretending the dates are the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of Nadia's payroll income to go in 2028, before we'd confirmed another income we could rely on. My own paid preparation could shrink too, with later robots competing for repair work, and my wage alone wouldn't meet our present mortgage and essential costs. I would wake at night adding the gap even with eleven months saved, because the gap could last much longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the AI question-card drafts now only with written employer approval, approved software, invented cases and no worker fees. Work must be in paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged, with my check and office verification before any customer use, stopping invented facts or repair instructions. I'd keep current offered repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures. During 2029 Nadia and I would use actual income records, costs, capacity and genuine paid offers before any affordable exit we both agreed, counting no assumed payment or new income from the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected missing payroll wage, while still able to ask a specific question and test a bounded idea. I wouldn't call the reserve worthless, but I wouldn't let eleven months answer a question about the rest of our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would completing the question-card trial replace the payroll income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a useful workflow doesn't put a second wage into our home account. A better question card isn't a replacement for my partner's payroll wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the household need before choosing an exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use verified amounts and dates, actual living costs and any work genuinely offered within my licence, competence and safe physical ability then. We'd have to agree the choice was affordable, not borrow a grown child's possible wage to make the page balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be sixty-eight at the thinking change in 2036 and seventy-one when robots follow around 2039. I'd use the decade to find out what choices we actually had, not promise thirteen more years of physical work. The small workflow would still be for today's calls, not a contract with my older self.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearer risk is still Nadia's payroll hours changing before full AGI, with my wage alone insufficient for our present costs. Our reserve and the many nearby firms give us room, but don't guarantee a second wage or a future vacancy. I can't know our income, physical capacity or retirement affordability at sixty-eight or seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona

Work must stay in paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged, with my check and office verification before customer use, stopping invented facts or repair instructions. I'd keep current offered repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures. During 2037 Nadia and I would review actual income records, costs, capacity and genuinely offered paid options before any affordable exit we both agreed, counting neither a job at sixty-nine nor a child's wage without an actual agreed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about earlier household changes, without feeling rushed by the physical robot date itself. I'd like the extra time to give us better questions, not a false income figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on the same kind of repairs at the later ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, any repair task would have to be genuinely offered, paid and within my licence, competence and safe physical capacity then. The customers I have now haven't booked my hands for seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children cover any gap in the later figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only help offered freely and actually agreed with their own needs considered could count. Our children may need help themselves, and I won't turn a family conversation into an unpaid contract.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I expect a large loss of Nadia's payroll income before another dependable household income is confirmed, with repair robots following around 2031. I'd lose sleep over the mortgage gap even while the eleven-month reserve gave us time to act. Written weekly wages and hours, protected paid testing of a small idea and verified actual later income figures would help more than being told liking AI made our household safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to say the new process didn't help. I want the office colleague to be able to reject a card that makes a real call harder, and I want that answer counted too. A trial should leave room for the worker who says the old question was clearer.

headlineQuote: A trial should leave room for the worker who says the old question was clearer.
portrait: Emeka is **fifty-eight**, an experienced average electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs without master or leadership standing.
His **higher pay** and partner Nadia's payroll wage cover current costs, with a mortgage, eleven months saved and plentiful nearby electrical employers.
His **daily checked AI notes** continue; a new question-card workflow requires approval, invented cases, paid shifts, protected weekly wages and before-use checks.
He expects **major payroll-income loss** in the fast picture, checking real later resources without choosing Nadia's career or assuming children's payments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected major payroll-income loss before replacement income is confirmed, with later repair robots around 2031 and sleeplessness.
whatWouldHelp: Provide **written weekly wages** and hours, protected paid testing and verified later income figures without treating a trial as replacement earnings.
